title: “IF YOUR RIGHT HAND CAUSES YOU TO SIN, CUT IT OFF” — THE TERRIFYING MERCY BEHIND JESUS’ WORDS
paragraphs: “IF YOUR RIGHT HAND CAUSES YOU TO SIN, CUT IT OFF” — THE TERRIFYING MERCY BEHIND JESUS’ WORDS
Jesus was not commanding you to mutilate your body. He was exposing something far more frightening: how desperately we protect the very things that are destroying our souls.
There are words of Jesus we frame and hang on walls.
“Come to Me.”
“Peace I leave with you.”
“Let the little children come to Me.”
And then there are words of Jesus that make the room suddenly uncomfortable.
Words we read twice because we secretly hope we misunderstood them.
“If your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off.”
What do you do with a sentence like that?
Because Jesus said it.
Not an angry medieval preacher.
Not a religious fanatic.
Jesus.
The same Jesus who touched lepers.
The same Jesus who welcomed sinners.
The same Jesus who wept beside a grave, forgave His enemies, restored failures, defended the broken, and eventually stretched His own hands across a Roman cross.
That Jesus said:
“Cut it off.”
And perhaps the reason these words disturb us so deeply is not because we cannot understand them.
Perhaps we understand them more than we want to admit.
Because somewhere inside your life there may already be something you know needs to go.
Not your literal hand.
Something you keep reaching for with it.
A conversation.
A relationship.
An app.
A browser window.
A private account.
A secret habit.
A compromise nobody knows about.
A fantasy you keep feeding.
A resentment you keep rehearsing.
A person whose attention has become more important to you than obedience to Christ.
Something that feels so connected to your life that losing it feels almost like losing part of yourself.
And Jesus looks directly at the thing we keep excusing and says, in effect:
You cannot make peace with what is trying to destroy you.
That is the severity behind His words.
But buried inside that severity is extraordinary mercy.
Matthew records Jesus saying:
“καὶ εἰ ἡ δεξιά σου χεὶρ σκανδαλίζει σε, ἔκκοψον αὐτὴν καὶ βάλε ἀπὸ σοῦ…”
Kai ei hē dexia sou cheir skandalizei se, ekkopson autēn kai bale apo sou…
The sense is:
“And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you.”
Look carefully at one word.
σκανδαλίζει — skandalizei.
It is related to the language of stumbling, ensnaring, or becoming an occasion for falling.
Jesus is describing something that becomes spiritually destructive—something through which you repeatedly stumble into sin.
Then comes the shocking imperative:
ἔκκοψον — ekkopson.
Cut it off.
Jesus intentionally chooses severe imagery because sin is not harmless.

He is not teaching bodily mutilation as the cure for sinful desire. In fact, only moments earlier, Jesus has moved the discussion precisely in the opposite direction—from merely external behavior into the human heart.
He says that adultery is not merely something committed physically. Lustful intent matters before God.
That changes everything.
You could remove a hand and still possess a sinful heart.
You could lose an eye and still lust.
You could throw away a phone and still crave what the phone once delivered.
You could move cities and carry the same bitterness with you.
You could leave the relationship and continue worshiping the memory of it.
Jesus is going deeper than anatomy.
He is coming after allegiance.
He is telling us that whatever repeatedly draws us toward rebellion against God must not be treated casually simply because separating from it hurts.
And this is where Christianity becomes painfully personal.
We love the idea of surrender until Jesus touches something we actually want.
We sing, “I surrender all,” and sometimes what we mean is:
I surrender everything except this.
Jesus, You can have Sunday.
You can have my worship songs.
You can have my public testimony.
You can have the Bible verses I post.
But don't touch this relationship.
Don't touch this habit.
Don't touch my pride.
Don't touch my pornography.
Don't touch my anger.
Don't touch my secret messages.
Don't touch my money.
Don't touch the approval I crave.
Don't touch the grudge that makes me feel powerful.
Don't touch the thing I already know is pulling me away from You.
And suddenly the words of Christ become frighteningly relevant.
“If your right hand causes you to stumble…”
Your right hand.
Not something obviously useless.
Something valuable.
Something familiar.
Something you depend upon.
Something you would hate to lose.
Jesus deliberately creates an image of painful separation because genuine repentance sometimes costs something.
There are moments when obedience feels like amputation.
You delete the number and your heart screams.
You end the affair and loneliness rushes into the empty space.
You confess the addiction and your carefully maintained image collapses.
You install accountability software because you finally admit willpower has not been enough.
You stop going somewhere because you know what happens when you go there.
You surrender the relationship because affection does not transform disobedience into holiness.
You apologize even though your pride begs you not to.
You return what should never have been yours.
You tell somebody the truth.
You remove access.
You establish boundaries.
You walk away.
And for a while it hurts.
That does not necessarily mean you made the wrong decision.
Sometimes obedience hurts because the thing being removed had roots.
We have become remarkably skilled at negotiating with those roots.
We rename bondage so we can tolerate it.
“It’s just how I cope.”
“We’re only talking.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“God understands.”
“Everybody struggles with this.”
“It isn’t hurting anyone.”
“I’ll deal with it eventually.”
But Jesus does not say, “Manage it.”
He says:
Cut it off.
Throw it away.
There is urgency in those verbs.
Not because Jesus enjoys taking things from you.
Because Jesus knows where unrepented sin leads.
That is the part modern ears often want removed from the passage.
Jesus continues by warning about γέεννα — Gehenna.
This is not motivational language.
Jesus is speaking about judgment.
The One who offers grace also warns us about sin because grace never required Jesus to pretend sin was harmless.
Look at the cross.
If sin were trivial, Calvary makes no sense.
If humanity merely needed encouragement, the Son of God did not need nails.
If our deepest problem were low self-esteem, Christ did not need to shed His blood.
The cross simultaneously declares two realities we desperately need to hear:
Your sin is more serious than you want to believe.
And God's mercy is greater than you dared to hope.
That is why Jesus can speak with such severity.
The Physician who knows the disease is terminal does not whisper about the tumor because He is afraid of upsetting the patient.
He tells the truth because He intends to save.
Imagine a surgeon discovering something deadly inside you.
You wake after surgery and discover that something was removed.
You ask why.
And the surgeon says:
“Because leaving it there would have killed you.”
You might grieve what was lost.
But eventually you understand.
The scar is evidence that somebody took your survival seriously.
Perhaps there are spiritual scars in your future.
A friendship you had to leave.
A relationship you could not continue.
A habit you finally confessed.
A lifestyle you stopped defending.
A possession you surrendered.
A door you permanently closed.
People may even ask why you became “so extreme.”
And perhaps your answer will simply be:
Because I finally understood that Jesus was worth more.
This is where we must be careful.
Radical repentance is not the same as earning salvation.
You do not cut sin from your life so God will finally love you.
You fight sin because in Christ you have encountered a love worth surrendering everything for.
Christianity is not:
Clean yourself up, and perhaps Jesus will accept you.
The Gospel is:
Jesus Christ came for sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went to the cross bearing sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And now the risen Christ calls sinners to repent, believe, follow Him, and walk in newness of life.
Grace does not tell sin, “You may stay.”
Grace tells the sinner:
“You don't have to remain its slave.”
That distinction matters.
Because somebody reading this has tried to quit.
Again.
And again.
And again.
You cried.
You promised God.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You blocked the number.
Then unblocked it.
You confessed.
Then fell again.
And now shame is whispering something poisonous:
“See? You're hopeless.”
No.
Your repeated failure is not permission to stop fighting.
Run back to Christ.
Confess again.
Bring the darkness into light.
Ask trusted mature believers for help.
Remove access.
Stop protecting your secrecy.
Repentance is not pretending you never fell.
Repentance turns toward Christ instead of building a home in the place where you fell.
Maybe you have spent years asking Jesus to take away a temptation while refusing to remove the doorway through which you repeatedly enter it.
Maybe you pray:
“Lord, keep me pure.”
Then you keep the private account.
“Lord, heal my marriage.”
Then you continue the hidden conversation.
“Lord, free me from pornography.”
Then you insist nobody needs to know.
“Lord, help me forgive.”
Then every night you replay the offense until anger feels like an old friend.
“Lord, make me holy.”
But don't touch this.
And perhaps Jesus' words have found you today because He loves you too much to help you decorate your chains.
Cut it off.
Not your body.
The access.
The arrangement.
The excuse.
The secret.
The pathway.
The compromise.
The provision you keep making for the flesh.
Whatever must go so that you can pursue Christ faithfully—stop calling it too expensive when Jesus is telling you your soul matters more.
And hear this carefully:
Your hand is not your savior.
Your discipline is not your savior.
Your accountability partner is not your savior.
Your tears are not your savior.
Your ability to maintain a perfect streak is not your savior.
Jesus Christ is.
Radical measures against sin cannot regenerate the human heart.
Christ must.
That is why Christianity cannot ultimately be reduced to “stop doing bad things.”
You need forgiveness.
You need reconciliation with God.
You need grace.
You need a new heart.
You need Christ.
And there is something breathtakingly beautiful about the Gospel when placed beside Matthew 5:30.
Jesus tells us to remove what leads us toward destruction.
Then later, Jesus Himself goes toward a cross to rescue sinners who did not remove sin perfectly.
Think about those hands.
The hands that touched the unclean.
The hands that broke bread for hungry crowds.
The hands that lifted sinking Peter.
The hands that washed His disciples' feet.
The hands that should have been worshiped by every human being alive.
Those hands were pierced.
Not because Jesus sinned.
Because we did.
The innocent One stood where the guilty belonged.
That does not make sin less serious.
It reveals just how serious sin was—and just how far divine love was willing to go to redeem sinners.
This is why the Christian story is never merely scandal.
It is scandal invaded by grace.
Peter denied Him.
Grace found Peter.
The thief was dying beside Him.
Grace opened paradise.
Saul persecuted His people.
Grace turned the persecutor into a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
Again and again Scripture tells the same impossible story.
Sin does not get the final word when Jesus enters the story.
Shame does not get the final word.
Your worst night does not get the final word.
Your addiction does not get the final word.
Your affair does not get the final word.
Your failure does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
But grace is not permission to return lovingly to the chains Christ came to break.
So now comes the question no one else can answer for you.
What is your “right hand”?
What have you been protecting that Jesus has been asking you to surrender?
Don't answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Maybe you already know.
Maybe your stomach tightened several paragraphs ago.
Maybe a name appeared in your mind.
Maybe a hidden habit did.
Maybe something inside you has been saying:
Not that.
Anything but that.
And perhaps that is exactly where the battle is.
Bring it to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you become stronger.
Not after one final time.
Now.
You may discover that what feels like losing your life is actually Christ leading you out of something that has been quietly consuming it.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought you could never escape, tell part of that testimony. Somebody reading quietly at 2:00 in the morning may need to discover that Christians struggle, fall, repent, receive grace, get back up, and keep following Jesus.
Not because every sentence was comfortable.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.

But if Gospel-centered teaching has helped you, supporting and sharing Gospel Warrior can help put biblical truth in front of another person who may desperately need it. Glorifying God is bigger than supporting any ministry; yet supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way of participating in spreading His Word.
Send this privately to the believer who has been fighting a battle nobody else sees.
It is not a shortcut to spiritual maturity.
Because somewhere in your circle is someone smiling publicly while losing a private war.
Someone is hiding.
Someone is exhausted.
Someone believes their secret has already disqualified them.
Someone needs to hear the terrifying mercy inside the words of Jesus:
Sin is serious enough to cut off every road that keeps carrying you back to it.
Grace is powerful enough to receive the sinner who finally comes home.
And Jesus is precious enough to lose anything rather than lose yourself chasing something that can never save you.
The hand was never the deepest problem.
The heart was.
And the answer was never mutilation.
The answer is surrender.
Repentance.
Grace.
A Savior.
Jesus Christ.
So whatever Christ is calling you to throw away, remember what remains when it is gone.
Him.
And if you still have Jesus, you have not lost your greatest treasure.
Sometimes the thing you are terrified to surrender is the very thing standing between your chains and the freedom Christ has been calling you into.
